headline: Medium prompt-injection and cascading-error risk from shared filesystem/stdin paths; no direct evidence of a blocking provenance layer.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Airflow can call APIs and has broad network egress, while xonsh reads files/stdin and writes the filesystem. That creates a plausible path where Airflow-produced content is saved and later interpreted by xonsh as commands or instructions. No provenance or isolation mechanism is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Airflow outputs are copied into files or stdin consumed by xonsh
IF xonsh executes content from shared workspace files without sanitization
mitigations: Keep Airflow outputs in a separate directory from xonsh inputs
Disable automatic execution of generated shell snippets
Add a manual review step before xonsh runs any Airflow-produced text
Use read-only mounts for Airflow output folders
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between producer and consumer

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airflow has broad network egress and xonsh reads filesystem contents, environment variables, and notebooks. If they share a workspace, xonsh can expose sensitive local artifacts while Airflow can transmit them outward. The profiles do not show secrets handling or isolation strong enough to rule this out, so the shared-workspace path is the best-supported default risk.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem workspace
IF xonsh reads files that contain secrets, notebooks, or environment variables
mitigations: Separate workspaces for orchestration and shell execution
Restrict xonsh to a least-privilege directory
Redact secrets from files before Airflow can access them
Audit outbound destinations for Airflow jobs
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Airflow can orchestrate networked automation, and xonsh can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write files. Even without modify_git_state, both can mutate the same filesystem and run concurrent actions. Because xonsh does not support multiple instances and no locking is documented, conflict risk is real in default shared-workspace setups.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF Airflow-triggered tasks and xonsh commands run concurrently
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize writes with a simple lock file
Run one agent at a time for shared resources
Make shared files append-only where possible
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airflow can generate or route task outputs, and xonsh can execute shell commands and subprocesses. If xonsh consumes Airflow output as authoritative input, a bad upstream result can cascade into incorrect commands or file writes. No verification or approval step is documented, so the pair supports a default propagation path.
conditions: IF xonsh treats Airflow-produced text as commands or parameters
IF there is no human or programmatic verification step between them
mitigations: Require explicit approval before xonsh acts on Airflow output
Validate Airflow outputs against a schema
Log and diff proposed commands before execution
Limit xonsh to dry-run mode for generated actions
requires-engineering: add typed contracts between agents

E_compliance.rationale: The profiles do not identify regulated data classes, residency constraints, or retention policies for either Airflow or xonsh. With no documented compliance mismatch, a residency or certification breach is not evidenced here. I cite both profiles because the absence of such fields in each is relevant to ruling out a specific compliance pathway.
conditions: IF future deployments route regulated data through either agent
IF one agent is assigned a stricter residency or retention policy than the other
mitigations: Document data-class handling for both agents
Confirm retention settings before deployment
Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement and audit logging
